GenScore: Agent-Based Short-Answer Question Generation and Scoring in Software Engineering Courses 

## TA NGUYEN BINH DUONG AND LWIN KHIN SHAR , (Member, IEEE) 

School of Computing and Information Systems, Singapore Management University, Singapore 188065 

Corresponding author: Ta Nguyen Binh Duong (donta@smu.edu.sg) 

**ABSTRACT** Short-answer questions are commonly used in educational assessments, as they are often viewed as a more effective way than multiple-choice questions to determine whether students have achieved the intended learning outcomes. However, manually creating appropriate questions targeting different cognitive levels such as those defined by the Bloom’s Taxonomy, and grading text answers from students are not trivial tasks for instructors. Existing work on auto-question generation and scoring in computing education typically targets coding-based questions. However, in software engineering courses, assessments can extend beyond coding to understanding of processes, DevOps methodologies, system design, etc. This work aims to address the dual problem of auto-generating and auto-scoring text based short-answer questions in software engineering courses. We propose an agent-based approach to question generation and scoring, in which each agent performs a distinct task and communicates with each other to complete its tasks. An agent can be realized using a selected large language model (LLM). To this end, we have implemented the proposed approach into a fully functional web app, utilizing OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o models, which was deployed to support instructors and students in our course. We conducted a thorough evaluation of the agent-based approach using several public and private datasets. The results demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach. Among other insights, we observed that the LLM agents are good at generating questions at Bloom’s cognitive levels of _Remember_ , _Understand_ , _Apply_ , and _Analyze_ ; and are good at scoring students’ answers when provided with 3 or more actual examples of human scoring. 

- **INDEX TERMS** Agent based systems, large language models, short-answer questions, auto-scoring, question generation. 

## **I. INTRODUCTION** 

Assessments in education can make use of multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, coding tests, essay writing, etc. While options such as multiple-choice questions are great for large cohorts in which evaluation speed and consistency are needed, short-answer questions are useful when you need evidence that students can recall or analyze key steps or concepts covered in the course [1]. For such questions, students will usually need to provide answers in several lines of text in an open-ended format. In many

For instance, in the software engineering course taught by the first author, in which foundational knowledge and theoretical aspects of software engineering are more important, students can be asked a short-answer question such as _briefly define continuous integration_ , which is at the _Remember (Recall)_ cognitive level of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. On the other hand, a question such as _Given a team that frequently misses sprint goals, determine whether Scrum is suitable and briefly justify your recommendation_ is clearly at a higher cognitive level ( _Evaluate_ ) which requires more than just the ability to recall facts. 

However, creating quality short-answer questions as described above and grading text answers from students manually can take a lot of time. Furthermore, students often want to practice on-demand, i.e., whenever they have the time, and require immediate feedback. For creating questions, instructors may wish to cater to students with varying levels of competency in a course, so the questions should be personalized at appropriate Bloom’s Taxonomy levels. In addition, as such short-answer questions can have several possible answers which can be entirely or partially correct, manual scoring in this case is a tedious and time-consuming process [6]. This has been the challenge for software engineering courses at our institution where the number of computing students has been increasing steadily, which may also apply to many other institutions due to the increasing demand for IT professionals worldwide [7]. 

There has not been much research in auto-generating short-answer questions recently. In [8], the authors described the application of large language models (LLMs) and knowledge graphs to generate the questions and answers for cybersecurity training. In [9], questions were generated for content in Spanish textbooks and evaluated by subject matter experts. In another recent study [10], the authors used LLMs (GPT-4) to generate Bloom’s Taxonomy-aligned multiplechoice questions (not short-answer) for a college-level biology course. We have not come across works on autogenerating short-answer questions for software engineering courses. 

On the other hand, auto-scoring of short textual answers is a well-known problem in technology-enabled education. Many existing approaches made use of traditional machine learning techniques [11], [12], [13]. These approaches need to incorporate feature engineering and model training. Recent approaches used deep learning to reduce the effort of manual feature engineering, but deep learning requires a significant amount of quality data to work well. More recently, researchers have been using LLMs such as OpenAI’s GPT family of models to perform auto-scoring of open-ended answers, e.g., [14], [15], [16], [17], and [18]. However, not much work has been done for LLM-based 

auto-scoring of short answers in the context of computing education, especially in theory-oriented software engineering courses. Such courses cover a wide range of topics including processes, software design, automation and quality practices, etc. Short-answer questions in these topics could have many different correct or partially correct solutions. We note that auto-scoring methods in computing education typically focus on programming based questions [19], which could be evaluated by executing a suite of test cases. 

This study attempts to address a real-world bottleneck in education in general: by automating both question generation and answer scoring, educators can deliver personalized assessments to a large number of students, and at the same time ensure that students receive immediate feedback needed for effective learning. Such automated systems have the potential to maintain objective grading standards. They can also enable educators to focus on other important activities such as curriculum design, personalized mentoring, etc. In this paper, we make the following major contributions: 

- We consider the dual problem of auto-generating questions and auto-scoring short-answers in the context of more theory-oriented software engineering courses. We target courses that focus on software processes and DevOps methodology aspects of software engineering rather than programming topics, which have been studied more extensively from an assessment point of view. 

- We propose an agent-based approach to question generation and scoring. Multiple agents are deployed in our system in which each performs a distinct function, communicates with each other to complete the generation or scoring task. In this work, an agent can be realized using a selected LLM, e.g., one of the OpenAI GPT models. Each agent is able to make use of suitable tools, e.g., file search, to complete its tasks. 

- We design and implement a fully functional web based system, called GenScore, for our agent based approach. The system supports both instructors and students. Instructors can use the system to quickly generate questions and quizzes; while students can practice question answering on-demand with instant grading. 

- We conduct an extensive evaluation of our approach using three datasets — a public dataset which has been widely used in short-answer scoring and two of our own datasets. We make use of a mixed-method strategy in this study which evaluates the performance of our approach both quantitatively and qualitatively. For the qualitative evaluation, a subject human expert assesses the quality of AI-generated outputs manually through many rounds of reviews. The results show the viability of our approach and provide further insights for future work in question generation and auto-scoring for various courses.

## **II. BACKGROUND** 

Generating and scoring open-ended, short-answer questions is a challenging problem as we need to ensure that they not only cover basic knowledge acquisition but also foster higher-order cognitive skills. As a metric to evaluate the generation-scoring efficacy, we leverage the widely-used Bloom’s Taxonomy [4]. In education, the Bloom’s Taxonomy organizes cognitive development into six hierarchical levels (or categories), namely _Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create_ . _Remember_ is about recalling facts or terminology covered in the course; _Understand_ requires students to explain or interpret known facts and terms; _Apply_ asks students to put knowledge into usage in new contexts; _Analyze_ requires students to break information into components and explore relationships between them, e.g., decomposing and analyzing a case study; _Evaluate_ assesses critical judgment of students given some criteria; lastly, _Create_ challenges students to synthesize and combine known elements to form new solutions. The Bloom’s Taxonomy has been applied to learning design and assessment in computer science education [20]. Here we show a few examples extracted from our course to illustrate how questions and answers under different Bloom levels can differ: 

_Remember._ Ask students to list a value of the Agile Manifesto, for which the answer could simply be: _working software over comprehensive documentation_ . 

_Understand._ Ask students to explain what the above Agile value means, for which the answer could be more elaborated and take more effort, such as: _Documentation should not delay the early and frequent delivery of a usable product_ . 

_Apply._ Ask students to write user stories with proper acceptance criteria. 

_Analyze._ Ask students to look at deployment log to identify process issues. 

_Evaluate._ Ask students to criticize the choices of container orchestration tools. 

_Create._ Ask students to propose a new way for measuring technical debts and its effects on team performance in a hypothetical organization. 

## **III. PROPOSED APPROACH** 

Our approach aims to address the problem of generating valid, clear, and relevant short-answer questions; and to perform automatic scoring of the answers given by students 

in our software engineering course, so that they can practice and get instant feedback. In the following, we describe our approach called GenScore. 

## _A. DESIGN_ 

The design of the GenScore system is shown in Figure 1. It has four types of agents, namely _Generation Agent_ , _Refinement Agent_ , _Rating Agent(s)_ , and _Scoring Agent(s)_ , each performing a distinct function and communicating with other agents in the system to complete the given task, i.e., question generation or scoring. An agent can be realized using a selected LLM [21]. In our implementation, we use OpenAI Assistants API, which enables each agent to use selected tools for its operations. For instance, our agents make use of file search for relevant context extraction from data sources such as lecture notes and other course materials, and JSON encoding so that each pair of generated question and answer can be extracted individually. 

In GenScore, instructors use a web interface to generate questions, by submitting keywords and a Bloom’s category as inputs. The _Generation Agent_ automatically creates preliminary short-answer questions and reference answers based on the given keywords, Bloom’s category, and selected course materials. The _Refinement Agent_ then applies predefined quality criteria to improve each question. Finally, one or more _Rating Agents_ evaluate the refined questions and reference answers using the same criteria used by the Refinement Agent. Questions passing a rating threshold, along with their model answers, are stored in the question bank for students to attempt later. By decomposing the question generation process into multiple stages, the system allows each agent in a stage to be more focused and effective on its tasks [22].

## _E. SCORING AGENTS_ 

For a given pair of question and student answer to be scored, the Scoring Agent uses a few-shot prompt [25] with examples extracted from the human-graded answers, as shown in Listing 5. For better representation of examples, they are selected from three different score categories, i.e., low score, medium score, and high score [14]. The Scoring Agent can be instructed to make use of suitable tools, e.g., file search, to incorporate relevant context from the lecture notes into the prompt if needed. As using a single Scoring Agent may produce inconsistencies in predicted scores due to the stochastic nature of LLMs, we propose the use of multiple independent Scoring Agents in scoring the same answer. The final score is the average of all the individual scores produced by each agent.

## _B. PERFORMANCE MEASURES_ 

## 1) EVALUATING QUESTION GENERATION PERFORMANCE 

For a consistent evaluation of the generated questions and reference answers, a single human rater (the 1st author of this paper) with significant experience in teaching software engineering evaluated all of them and provided a score based on the same criteria used by the Rating Agents: 

- 1) **Validity of question** : whether the question is set correctly and belongs to the requested category of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

- 2) **Validity of answers** : whether all of the reference answers are correct and belong to the requested category of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

- 3) **Clarity of question** : whether the question is clear and concise. 

- 4) **Clarity of answers** : whether all the reference answers are clear and concise. 

- 5) **Relevance of question** : whether the question is within the scope of the specified lecture notes. 

- 6) **Relevance of answers** : whether all the answers are within the scope of the specified lecture notes. 

The human rater awarded a maximum of two points for each of the 6 criteria above, for a total of 12 points. Points were awarded depending on how well the question and its reference answers meet each criterion: 

- 1) **Not at all: 0 point** . For example, a question designated for the Create category, but asks student to recall a concept will be given 0 point for Validity. 

- 2) **Partially satisfactory: 1 point** . The question or answers might have some minor issues which require further modification before use. For example, some reference answers generated in our experiments, especially those under the Create category, provided additional details not covered in the lecture notes at all. 

- 3) **Entirely satisfactory: 2 points** . The question or answers are without any issues and can be used right away with no further modification. 

To mitigate the issue of not having a second rater, the following step-by-step evaluation process was followed to ensure the consistency of the ratings produced by the single human rater. 

- 1) The rater focuses on a single course topic at a time, such as software testing, to facilitate more accurate Bloom category assignment through comparison of questions within the same topic. 

- 2) The rater begins with questions in the simplest unrated Bloom category, Remember, which is one of the easiest cognitive levels to identify. The rater reads each question and evaluates its reference answers to assess validity, including correctness and appropriate Bloom category assignment. Points (0, 1, or 2) are then given accordingly. 

- 3) The rater then evaluates the clarity (clear, conciseness) of the question and answers. Points are given accordingly. 

- 4) The rater then refers to the relevant lecture notes to determine whether the question falls within the course scope and assigns points accordingly. 

- 5) After completing ratings for all questions within the same topic and Bloom category, the rater compares these questions and their ratings both against each other and against questions from the immediately preceding Bloom category to identify potential discrepancies. For example, an Apply question must assess students at a higher cognitive level than Understand by testing how they use information in new situations rather than just explaining concepts. The rater then adjusts the ratings if needed. 

- 6) The rater moves to the next Bloom category, e.g., Understand, in the same course topic and repeats steps 2-5.

## _D. THREATS TO VALIDITY_ 

Like other empirical studies, the generalizability of our results is subject to a few threats as discussed below. 

First, this study employed a single human rater for the manual evaluation of generated questions. The rater is highly experienced in software engineering educational assessments. Such expertise, especially in highly specialized domains like software engineering education, can provide reliable evaluation of outputs generated by the agents in GenScore. However, we also recognized that including a second rater (who was not available to us during the time of the experiments) and reporting inter-rater metrics such as Krippendorff’s alpha might strengthen the reliability of this study. 

Second, outputs from LLMs could be changing from time to time due to their probabilistic nature. This would affect the quality of question generation, the rating of questions and the auto-scoring accuracy. We have mitigated this issue by generating and evaluating more than 300 new questions across 8 popular topics in software engineering and 6 different Bloom’s cognitive levels. We also used three different datasets with a total of more than 2800 answers to be auto-scored. At the same time, we recognize the importance of conducting the evaluation with more real-world datasets containing questions set at the higher cognitive levels of the Bloom categories, especially for the auto-scoring performance. Such datasets in software engineering courses are not available to us at the moment. 

Third, due to the budget and time constraints, we could not fully implement and evaluate the latest LLM models such as the reasoning models [38]. Newer and more expensive LLM models might improve the generation and auto-scoring performance compared to what have been reported in this 

work. As an extension of this work, we plan to run experiments with the latest LLM models such as OpenAI’s GPT-5 when the cost becomes more manageable and study if it improves the performance of rating agents when dealing with the higher cognitive levels of Bloom categories. In addition, we also plan to build rubric-based generators or discriminator enhancements designed specifically for higher Bloom levels such as _Evaluate_ and _Create_ , to improve our current rating agents. Such enhancements may produce better agreement between the human rater and the LLM-based agents. We note this area as an opportunity for possible improvement in our upcoming studies. 

Finally, we acknowledge that GenScore is primarily a proof of concept system. We plan to make it production-ready and evaluate it further in terms of system scalability and usability in real classroom deployments. In order not to cause possibly significant disruptions in student learning, such deployments will be complementary to existing classroom practices, i.e., students will have GenScore as an additional tool to practice new short answer questions in their own pace and get instant feedback. Based on the experimental results, we believe that it is necessary to include expert human oversight over practice questions generated by the system under the higher Bloom cognitive levels.

Auto-generating assessments is an established research topic in technology-enabled education [39]. Existing work in this area have been focusing on various educational domains, such as reading comprehension question generation using natural language processing techniques [40], and more recently LLM based programming exercise generation [41], [42]. The study evaluated 120 generated questions, but they were essay-type, not short-answer type of questions. There have been recent research on the effectiveness of LLMs in generating assessment questions based on taxonomies such as Bloom’s. We noted that deep learning based approaches require large, high quality datasets for proper model training and evaluation. 

With the recent rise of LLMs, naturally there have been more work on using them to perform auto-scoring of openended answers, for instance [14], [15], [16], [17]. Ta et al. In other educational domains, Chang and Ginter [15] investigated the auto-scoring problem in Finnish based undergraduate courses using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. In [49], the authors implemented and evaluated few-shot pre-trained language models for the automatic essay scoring task. We noted that grading essays is quite different from short-answer scoring, as the former requires the evaluation of different criteria such as text coherence and organization, logical arguments, etc. The authors of [50] evaluated GPT-4 for short answer grading using the SciEntsBank and Beetle datasets. They found that for these datasets, GPT-4’s performance is comparable to manually crafted machine learning models. ChatGPT was used in [51] to correct open-ended answers in technical training of professional software developers. We noted that existing approaches did not attempt to investigate the auto-scoring performance with respect to various cognitive levels in the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

**Summary** : Our approach presents several main novelties over existing LLM-based educational tools. First, GenScore integrates question generation and auto-scoring in a unified system for software engineering education, whereas existing work treats these as separate problems. Second, we target short-answer questions aligned to Bloom’s Taxonomy for theory-oriented software engineering courses. Prior work has focused on other assessment formats (essays, multiple-choice, programming exercises) or other educational domains. Third, we evaluate both question generation quality and scoring performance across Bloom’s cognitive levels. Our experiments revealed that LLMs struggle more with creating questions for higher-order thinking skills such as Evaluate and Create in software engineering contexts. This taxonomy-based performance analysis for both generation and scoring has not been explored in prior research in automated assessments.

In this work, we developed a practical, automated short answer question generation and answer scoring system, named GenScore, which can be used by both instructors and students in the context of software engineering courses. GenScore involves the use of LLM agents which can perform complex tasks based on customized prompts and relevant tool usage, e.g., to extract context from suitable lecture notes for enhancing generation and scoring performance. In this way, GenScore can be used for question generation and scoring for a wide variety of courses if the relevant course materials are provided, not just for software engineering courses. 

We conducted extensive experiments to investigate the auto-generation and auto-scoring capabilities of GenScore. We used a large number of course topics and questions/answers from various datasets including publicly available and our own datasets. The results demonstrated

**ABSTRACT** Short-answer questions are commonly used in educational assessments, as they are often viewed as a more effective way than multiple-choice questions to determine whether students have achieved the intended learning outcomes. However, manually creating appropriate questions targeting different cognitive levels such as those defined by the Bloom’s Taxonomy, and grading text answers from students are not trivial tasks for instructors. Existing work on auto-question generation and scoring in computing education typically targets coding-based questions. However, in software engineering courses, assessments can extend beyond coding to understanding of processes, DevOps methodologies, system design, etc. This work aims to address the dual problem of auto-generating and auto-scoring text based short-answer questions in software engineering courses. We propose an agent-based approach to question generation and scoring, in which each agent performs a distinct task and communicates with each other to complete its tasks. An agent can be realized using a selected large language model (LLM). To this end, we have implemented the proposed approach into a fully functional web app, utilizing OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o models, which was deployed to support instructors and students in our course. We conducted a thorough evaluation of the agent-based approach using several public and private datasets. The results demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach. Among other insights, we observed that the LLM agents are good at generating questions at Bloom’s cognitive levels of _Remember_ , _Understand_ , _Apply_ , and _Analyze_ ; and are good at scoring students’ answers when provided with 3 or more actual examples of human scoring.

## **I. INTRODUCTION** 

Assessments in education can make use of multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, coding tests, essay writing, etc. While options such as multiple-choice questions are great for large cohorts in which evaluation speed and consistency are needed, short-answer questions are useful when you need evidence that students can recall or analyze key steps or concepts covered in the course [1]. For such questions, students will usually need to provide answers in several lines of text in an open-ended format. In many

However, creating quality short-answer questions as described above and grading text answers from students manually can take a lot of time. Furthermore, students often want to practice on-demand, i.e., whenever they have the time, and require immediate feedback. For creating questions, instructors may wish to cater to students with varying levels of competency in a course, so the questions should be personalized at appropriate Bloom’s Taxonomy levels. In addition, as such short-answer questions can have several possible answers which can be entirely or partially correct, manual scoring in this case is a tedious and time-consuming process [6]. This has been the challenge for software engineering courses at our institution where the number of computing students has been increasing steadily, which may also apply to many other institutions due to the increasing demand for IT professionals worldwide [7]. 

There has not been much research in auto-generating short-answer questions recently. In [8], the authors described the application of large language models (LLMs) and knowledge graphs to generate the questions and answers for cybersecurity training. In [9], questions were generated for content in Spanish textbooks and evaluated by subject matter experts. In another recent study [10], the authors used LLMs (GPT-4) to generate Bloom’s Taxonomy-aligned multiplechoice questions (not short-answer) for a college-level biology course. We have not come across works on autogenerating short-answer questions for software engineering courses. 

On the other hand, auto-scoring of short textual answers is a well-known problem in technology-enabled education. Many existing approaches made use of traditional machine learning techniques [11], [12], [13]. These approaches need to incorporate feature engineering and model training. Recent approaches used deep learning to reduce the effort of manual feature engineering, but deep learning requires a significant amount of quality data to work well. More recently, researchers have been using LLMs such as OpenAI’s GPT family of models to perform auto-scoring of open-ended answers, e.g., [14], [15], [16], [17], and [18]. However, not much work has been done for LLM-based 

auto-scoring of short answers in the context of computing education, especially in theory-oriented software engineering courses. Such courses cover a wide range of topics including processes, software design, automation and quality practices, etc. Short-answer questions in these topics could have many different correct or partially correct solutions. We note that auto-scoring methods in computing education typically focus on programming based questions [19], which could be evaluated by executing a suite of test cases. 

This study attempts to address a real-world bottleneck in education in general: by automating both question generation and answer scoring, educators can deliver personalized assessments to a large number of students, and at the same time ensure that students receive immediate feedback needed for effective learning. Such automated systems have the potential to maintain objective grading standards. They can also enable educators to focus on other important activities such as curriculum design, personalized mentoring, etc. In this paper, we make the following major contributions: 

- We consider the dual problem of auto-generating questions and auto-scoring short-answers in the context of more theory-oriented software engineering courses. We target courses that focus on software processes and DevOps methodology aspects of software engineering rather than programming topics, which have been studied more extensively from an assessment point of view. 

- We propose an agent-based approach to question generation and scoring. Multiple agents are deployed in our system in which each performs a distinct function, communicates with each other to complete the generation or scoring task. In this work, an agent can be realized using a selected LLM, e.g., one of the OpenAI GPT models. Each agent is able to make use of suitable tools, e.g., file search, to complete its tasks. 

- We design and implement a fully functional web based system, called GenScore, for our agent based approach. The system supports both instructors and students. Instructors can use the system to quickly generate questions and quizzes; while students can practice question answering on-demand with instant grading. 

- We conduct an extensive evaluation of our approach using three datasets — a public dataset which has been widely used in short-answer scoring and two of our own datasets. We make use of a mixed-method strategy in this study which evaluates the performance of our approach both quantitatively and qualitatively. For the qualitative evaluation, a subject human expert assesses the quality of AI-generated outputs manually through many rounds of reviews. The results show the viability of our approach and provide further insights for future work in question generation and auto-scoring for various courses.

## **II. BACKGROUND** 

Generating and scoring open-ended, short-answer questions is a challenging problem as we need to ensure that they not only cover basic knowledge acquisition but also foster higher-order cognitive skills. As a metric to evaluate the generation-scoring efficacy, we leverage the widely-used Bloom’s Taxonomy [4]. In education, the Bloom’s Taxonomy organizes cognitive development into six hierarchical levels (or categories), namely _Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create_ . _Remember_ is about recalling facts or terminology covered in the course; _Understand_ requires students to explain or interpret known facts and terms; _Apply_ asks students to put knowledge into usage in new contexts; _Analyze_ requires students to break information into components and explore relationships between them, e.g., decomposing and analyzing a case study; _Evaluate_ assesses critical judgment of students given some criteria; lastly, _Create_ challenges students to synthesize and combine known elements to form new solutions. ## **III. PROPOSED APPROACH** 

Our approach aims to address the problem of generating valid, clear, and relevant short-answer questions; and to perform automatic scoring of the answers given by students 

in our software engineering course, so that they can practice and get instant feedback. In the following, we describe our approach called GenScore. 

## _A. DESIGN_ 

The design of the GenScore system is shown in Figure 1. ## _B. PERFORMANCE MEASURES_ 

## 1) EVALUATING QUESTION GENERATION PERFORMANCE 

For a consistent evaluation of the generated questions and reference answers, a single human rater (the 1st author of this paper) with significant experience in teaching software engineering evaluated all of them and provided a score based on the same criteria used by the Rating Agents: 

- 1) **Validity of question** : whether the question is set correctly and belongs to the requested category of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

- 2) **Validity of answers** : whether all of the reference answers are correct and belong to the requested category of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

- 3) **Clarity of question** : whether the question is clear and concise. 

- 4) **Clarity of answers** : whether all the reference answers are clear and concise. 

- 5) **Relevance of question** : whether the question is within the scope of the specified lecture notes. 

- 6) **Relevance of answers** : whether all the answers are within the scope of the specified lecture notes. 

The human rater awarded a maximum of two points for each of the 6 criteria above, for a total of 12 points. Points were awarded depending on how well the question and its reference answers meet each criterion: 

- 1) **Not at all: 0 point** . For example, a question designated for the Create category, but asks student to recall a concept will be given 0 point for Validity. 

- 2) **Partially satisfactory: 1 point** . The question or answers might have some minor issues which require further modification before use. For example, some reference answers generated in our experiments, especially those under the Create category, provided additional details not covered in the lecture notes at all. 

- 3) **Entirely satisfactory: 2 points** . The question or answers are without any issues and can be used right away with no further modification. 

To mitigate the issue of not having a second rater, the following step-by-step evaluation process was followed to ensure the consistency of the ratings produced by the single human rater. 

- 1) The rater focuses on a single course topic at a time, such as software testing, to facilitate more accurate Bloom category assignment through comparison of questions within the same topic. 

- 2) The rater begins with questions in the simplest unrated Bloom category, Remember, which is one of the easiest cognitive levels to identify. The rater reads each question and evaluates its reference answers to assess validity, including correctness and appropriate Bloom category assignment. Points (0, 1, or 2) are then given accordingly. 

- 3) The rater then evaluates the clarity (clear, conciseness) of the question and answers. Points are given accordingly. 

- 4) The rater then refers to the relevant lecture notes to determine whether the question falls within the course scope and assigns points accordingly. 

- 5) After completing ratings for all questions within the same topic and Bloom category, the rater compares these questions and their ratings both against each other and against questions from the immediately preceding Bloom category to identify potential discrepancies. For example, an Apply question must assess students at a higher cognitive level than Understand by testing how they use information in new situations rather than just explaining concepts. The rater then adjusts the ratings if needed. 

- 6) The rater moves to the next Bloom category, e.g., Understand, in the same course topic and repeats steps 2-5.

## _D. THREATS TO VALIDITY_ 

Like other empirical studies, the generalizability of our results is subject to a few threats as discussed below. 

First, this study employed a single human rater for the manual evaluation of generated questions. The rater is highly experienced in software engineering educational assessments. Such expertise, especially in highly specialized domains like software engineering education, can provide reliable evaluation of outputs generated by the agents in GenScore. However, we also recognized that including a second rater (who was not available to us during the time of the experiments) and reporting inter-rater metrics such as Krippendorff’s alpha might strengthen the reliability of this study. 

Second, outputs from LLMs could be changing from time to time due to their probabilistic nature. This would affect the quality of question generation, the rating of questions and the auto-scoring accuracy. We have mitigated this issue by generating and evaluating more than 300 new questions across 8 popular topics in software engineering and 6 different Bloom’s cognitive levels. We also used three different datasets with a total of more than 2800 answers to be auto-scored. At the same time, we recognize the importance of conducting the evaluation with more real-world datasets containing questions set at the higher cognitive levels of the Bloom categories, especially for the auto-scoring performance. Such datasets in software engineering courses are not available to us at the moment. 

Third, due to the budget and time constraints, we could not fully implement and evaluate the latest LLM models such as the reasoning models [38]. Newer and more expensive LLM models might improve the generation and auto-scoring performance compared to what have been reported in this 

work. As an extension of this work, we plan to run experiments with the latest LLM models such as OpenAI’s GPT-5 when the cost becomes more manageable and study if it improves the performance of rating agents when dealing with the higher cognitive levels of Bloom categories. In addition, we also plan to build rubric-based generators or discriminator enhancements designed specifically for higher Bloom levels such as _Evaluate_ and _Create_ , to improve our current rating agents. Such enhancements may produce better agreement between the human rater and the LLM-based agents. We note this area as an opportunity for possible improvement in our upcoming studies. 

Finally, we acknowledge that GenScore is primarily a proof of concept system. We plan to make it production-ready and evaluate it further in terms of system scalability and usability in real classroom deployments. In order not to cause possibly significant disruptions in student learning, such deployments will be complementary to existing classroom practices, i.e., students will have GenScore as an additional tool to practice new short answer questions in their own pace and get instant feedback. Based on the experimental results, we believe that it is necessary to include expert human oversight over practice questions generated by the system under the higher Bloom cognitive levels. 

## **VII. RELATED WORK** 

Auto-generating assessments is an established research topic in technology-enabled education [39]. Existing work in this area have been focusing on various educational domains, such as reading comprehension question generation using natural language processing techniques [40], and more recently LLM based programming exercise generation [41], [42]. In [8], the authors applied LLMs and knowledge graphs to generate questions and answers for cybersecurity training. In [9], the authors performed automatic generation and evaluation of questions for content in Spanish. We have not come across works on auto-generating short-answer questions for software engineering courses. 

To the best of our knowledge, not much work has been done in generating short-answers questions that are aligned to the Bloom’s Taxonomy, which has been considered widely in educational assessment [43]. In [44], the authors investigated the problem of generating questions for the 6-level Boom’s Taxonomy based on the lecture material of an undergraduate software engineering course. The study evaluated 120 generated questions, but they were essay-type, not short-answer type of questions. In a more recent study [10], the authors used GPT-4 for Bloom-aligned multiple-choice, not shortanswer, question generation in a biology course. 

There have been recent research on the effectiveness of LLMs in generating assessment questions based on taxonomies such as Bloom’s. In [45], the authors conducted a human evaluation to assess the usefulness and quality of the questions generated by LLMs. The questions used in the evaluation were in the machine learning and biology domains, not software engineering. On the other hand, auto-scoring of short textual answers is a relatively more well-studied problem, especially with the recent development in LLMs [15]. Previous approaches made use of machine learning techniques [11], [12], [13], in which significant effort would be needed to manually engineer appropriate features for training the machine learning models. In [12], using the Mohler dataset [11] the authors considered different feature extraction techniques including text similarity, weights of terms, question demotion, etc., to develop regression models for auto-scoring short answers. In [13], various traditional machine learning models such as Random Forest and Support Vector Machines were trained on a subset of human-graded answers to classify the remaining answers. The results demonstrated significant reduction in manual workload in grading. Interestingly, in a recent work (2025), Boonsarngsuk et al. They achieved competitive performance compared to new LLM based approaches using OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini. Their datasets were collected from a Statistics and a Computer Architecture course at a university in Thailand. 

To reduce the manual feature engineering effort required in traditional machine learning, deep learning based methods for auto-scoring have become popular [32], [34], [36], [47]. Such models, e.g., text embedding, attention based neural networks, etc., have the ability to learn representative features directly from large datasets. In addition, manually crafted features could be incorporated in a complementary manner into deep learning models to enhance scoring accuracy [27]. We noted that deep learning based approaches require large, high quality datasets for proper model training and evaluation. 

With the recent rise of LLMs, naturally there have been more work on using them to perform auto-scoring of openended answers, for instance [14], [15], [16], [17]. Ta et al. [14] evaluated the performance of different OpenAI’s LLMs in scoring short-answer questions in software engineering courses, but did not consider an agent based approach nor the integration with question generation in a unified system to support learning. Other than that, not much work has been done for LLM-based auto-scoring of short answers in the context of computing education, especially in more theory-oriented software engineering courses. Research in auto-scoring of open-ended answers in computing education have been more involved with programming based questions [19], [48]. 

In other educational domains, Chang and Ginter [15] investigated the auto-scoring problem in Finnish based undergraduate courses using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The data was collected from different academic disciplines at the University of Turku. They found that GPT-4 (one-shot learning) provided the best performance. In [49], the authors implemented and evaluated few-shot pre-trained language models for the automatic essay scoring task. We noted that grading essays is quite different from short-answer scoring, as the former requires the evaluation of different criteria such as text coherence and organization, logical arguments, etc. The authors of [50] evaluated GPT-4 for short answer grading using the SciEntsBank and Beetle datasets. They found that for these datasets, GPT-4’s performance is comparable to manually crafted machine learning models. ChatGPT was used in [51] to correct open-ended answers in technical training of professional software developers. We noted that existing approaches did not attempt to investigate the auto-scoring performance with respect to various cognitive levels in the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

**Summary** : Our approach presents several main novelties over existing LLM-based educational tools. First, GenScore integrates question generation and auto-scoring in a unified system for software engineering education, whereas existing work treats these as separate problems. Second, we target short-answer questions aligned to Bloom’s Taxonomy for theory-oriented software engineering courses. Prior work has focused on other assessment formats (essays, multiple-choice, programming exercises) or other educational domains. Third, we evaluate both question generation quality and scoring performance across Bloom’s cognitive levels. Our experiments revealed that LLMs struggle more with creating questions for higher-order thinking skills such as Evaluate and Create in software engineering contexts. This taxonomy-based performance analysis for both generation and scoring has not been explored in prior research in automated assessments. 

## **VIII. CONCLUSION** 

In this work, we developed a practical, automated short answer question generation and answer scoring system, named GenScore, which can be used by both instructors and students in the context of software engineering courses. GenScore involves the use of LLM agents which can perform complex tasks based on customized prompts and relevant tool usage, e.g., to extract context from suitable lecture notes for enhancing generation and scoring performance. In this way, GenScore can be used for question generation and scoring for a wide variety of courses if the relevant course materials are provided, not just for software engineering courses. 

We conducted extensive experiments to investigate the auto-generation and auto-scoring capabilities of GenScore. We used a large number of course topics and questions/answers from various datasets including publicly available and our own datasets. The results demonstrated

sections.text:

Corresponding author: Ta Nguyen Binh Duong (donta@smu.edu.sg) 

**ABSTRACT** Short-answer questions are commonly used in educational assessments, as they are often viewed as a more effective way than multiple-choice questions to determine whether students have achieved the intended learning outcomes. However, manually creating appropriate questions targeting different cognitive levels such as those defined by the Bloom’s Taxonomy, and grading text answers from students are not trivial tasks for instructors. Existing work on auto-question generation and scoring in computing education typically targets coding-based questions. However, in software engineering courses, assessments can extend beyond coding to understanding of processes, DevOps methodologies, system design, etc. This work aims to address the dual problem of auto-generating and auto-scoring text based short-answer questions in software engineering courses. We propose an agent-based approach to question generation and scoring, in which each agent performs a distinct task and communicates with each other to complete its tasks. An agent can be realized using a selected large language model (LLM). To this end, we have implemented the proposed approach into a fully functional web app, utilizing OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o models, which was deployed to support instructors and students in our course. We conducted a thorough evaluation of the agent-based approach using several public and private datasets. The results demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach. Among other insights, we observed that the LLM agents are good at generating questions at Bloom’s cognitive levels of _Remember_ , _Understand_ , _Apply_ , and _Analyze_ ; and are good at scoring students’ answers when provided with 3 or more actual examples of human scoring. 

- **INDEX TERMS** Agent based systems, large language models, short-answer questions, auto-scoring, question generation.

sections.heading: **I. INTRODUCTION**
sections.text:
Assessments in education can make use of multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, coding tests, essay writing, etc. While options such as multiple-choice questions are great for large cohorts in which evaluation speed and consistency are needed, short-answer questions are useful when you need evidence that students can recall or analyze key steps or concepts covered in the course [1]. For such questions, students will usually need to provide answers in several lines of text in an open-ended format. In many

To be more effective in assessing learning, short-answer questions can be set at higher cognitive levels as specified by the Bloom’s Taxonomy [4], which has been used widely in education. Questions that target _Analyze_ , _Evaluate_ , and _Create_ (the top three tiers of the Bloom’s Taxonomy) help learners to acquire a deeper understanding, longterm retention of knowledge, and a development of critical thinking and problem solving skills [5]. These questions provide a better differentiation between students who can

only recall facts and those who can actually grasp the content. In this way, instructors can foster learners who can remember key concepts and can use them effectively in new situations. For instance, in the software engineering course taught by the first author, in which foundational knowledge and theoretical aspects of software engineering are more important, students can be asked a short-answer question such as _briefly define continuous integration_ , which is at the _Remember (Recall)_ cognitive level of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. On the other hand, a question such as _Given a team that frequently misses sprint goals, determine whether Scrum is suitable and briefly justify your recommendation_ is clearly at a higher cognitive level ( _Evaluate_ ) which requires more than just the ability to recall facts. 

However, creating quality short-answer questions as described above and grading text answers from students manually can take a lot of time. Furthermore, students often want to practice on-demand, i.e., whenever they have the time, and require immediate feedback. For creating questions, instructors may wish to cater to students with varying levels of competency in a course, so the questions should be personalized at appropriate Bloom’s Taxonomy levels. In addition, as such short-answer questions can have several possible answers which can be entirely or partially correct, manual scoring in this case is a tedious and time-consuming process [6]. This has been the challenge for software engineering courses at our institution where the number of computing students has been increasing steadily, which may also apply to many other institutions due to the increasing demand for IT professionals worldwide [7]. 

There has not been much research in auto-generating short-answer questions recently. In [8], the authors described the application of large language models (LLMs) and knowledge graphs to generate the questions and answers for cybersecurity training. In [9], questions were generated for content in Spanish textbooks and evaluated by subject matter experts. In another recent study [10], the authors used LLMs (GPT-4) to generate Bloom’s Taxonomy-aligned multiplechoice questions (not short-answer) for a college-level biology course. We have not come across works on autogenerating short-answer questions for software engineering courses. 

On the other hand, auto-scoring of short textual answers is a well-known problem in technology-enabled education. Many existing approaches made use of traditional machine learning techniques [11], [12], [13]. These approaches need to incorporate feature engineering and model training. Recent approaches used deep learning to reduce the effort of manual feature engineering, but deep learning requires a significant amount of quality data to work well. More recently, researchers have been using LLMs such as OpenAI’s GPT family of models to perform auto-scoring of open-ended answers, e.g., [14], [15], [16], [17], and [18]. However, not much work has been done for LLM-based 

auto-scoring of short answers in the context of computing education, especially in theory-oriented software engineering courses. Such courses cover a wide range of topics including processes, software design, automation and quality practices, etc. Short-answer questions in these topics could have many different correct or partially correct solutions. We note that auto-scoring methods in computing education typically focus on programming based questions [19], which could be evaluated by executing a suite of test cases. 

This study attempts to address a real-world bottleneck in education in general: by automating both question generation and answer scoring, educators can deliver personalized assessments to a large number of students, and at the same time ensure that students receive immediate feedback needed for effective learning. Such automated systems have the potential to maintain objective grading standards. They can also enable educators to focus on other important activities such as curriculum design, personalized mentoring, etc. In this paper, we make the following major contributions: 

- We consider the dual problem of auto-generating questions and auto-scoring short-answers in the context of more theory-oriented software engineering courses. We target courses that focus on software processes and DevOps methodology aspects of software engineering rather than programming topics, which have been studied more extensively from an assessment point of view. 

- We propose an agent-based approach to question generation and scoring. Multiple agents are deployed in our system in which each performs a distinct function, communicates with each other to complete the generation or scoring task. In this work, an agent can be realized using a selected LLM, e.g., one of the OpenAI GPT models. Each agent is able to make use of suitable tools, e.g., file search, to complete its tasks. 

- We design and implement a fully functional web based system, called GenScore, for our agent based approach. The system supports both instructors and students. Instructors can use the system to quickly generate questions and quizzes; while students can practice question answering on-demand with instant grading. 

- We conduct an extensive evaluation of our approach using three datasets — a public dataset which has been widely used in short-answer scoring and two of our own datasets. We make use of a mixed-method strategy in this study which evaluates the performance of our approach both quantitatively and qualitatively. For the qualitative evaluation, a subject human expert assesses the quality of AI-generated outputs manually through many rounds of reviews. The results show the viability of our approach and provide further insights for future work in question generation and auto-scoring for various courses.

sections.heading: **II. BACKGROUND**
sections.text:
Generating and scoring open-ended, short-answer questions is a challenging problem as we need to ensure that they not only cover basic knowledge acquisition but also foster higher-order cognitive skills. As a metric to evaluate the generation-scoring efficacy, we leverage the widely-used Bloom’s Taxonomy [4]. In education, the Bloom’s Taxonomy organizes cognitive development into six hierarchical levels (or categories), namely _Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create_ . _Remember_ is about recalling facts or terminology covered in the course; _Understand_ requires students to explain or interpret known facts and terms; _Apply_ asks students to put knowledge into usage in new contexts; _Analyze_ requires students to break information into components and explore relationships between them, e.g., decomposing and analyzing a case study; _Evaluate_ assesses critical judgment of students given some criteria; lastly, _Create_ challenges students to synthesize and combine known elements to form new solutions. _Remember._ Ask students to list a value of the Agile Manifesto, for which the answer could simply be: _working software over comprehensive documentation_ .

_Apply._ Ask students to write user stories with proper acceptance criteria.

_Evaluate._ Ask students to criticize the choices of container orchestration tools.

sections.heading: **III. PROPOSED APPROACH**
sections.text:
Our approach aims to address the problem of generating valid, clear, and relevant short-answer questions; and to perform automatic scoring of the answers given by students 

in our software engineering course, so that they can practice and get instant feedback. In the following, we describe our approach called GenScore.

sections.heading: _A. DESIGN_
sections.text:
The design of the GenScore system is shown in Figure 1. It has four types of agents, namely _Generation Agent_ , _Refinement Agent_ , _Rating Agent(s)_ , and _Scoring Agent(s)_ , each performing a distinct function and communicating with other agents in the system to complete the given task, i.e., question generation or scoring. An agent can be realized using a selected LLM [21]. In our implementation, we use OpenAI Assistants API, which enables each agent to use selected tools for its operations. For instance, our agents make use of file search for relevant context extraction from data sources such as lecture notes and other course materials, and JSON encoding so that each pair of generated question and answer can be extracted individually. 

In GenScore, instructors use a web interface to generate questions, by submitting keywords and a Bloom’s category as inputs. The _Generation Agent_ automatically creates preliminary short-answer questions and reference answers based on the given keywords, Bloom’s category, and selected course materials. The _Refinement Agent_ then applies predefined quality criteria to improve each question. Finally, one or more _Rating Agents_ evaluate the refined questions and reference answers using the same criteria used by the Refinement Agent. Questions passing a rating threshold, along with their model answers, are stored in the question bank for students to attempt later. By decomposing the question generation process into multiple stages, the system allows each agent in a stage to be more focused and effective on its tasks [22].

sections.heading: 1) EVALUATING QUESTION GENERATION PERFORMANCE
sections.text:
For a consistent evaluation of the generated questions and reference answers, a single human rater (the 1st author of this paper) with significant experience in teaching software engineering evaluated all of them and provided a score based on the same criteria used by the Rating Agents: 

- 1) **Validity of question** : whether the question is set correctly and belongs to the requested category of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

- 2) **Validity of answers** : whether all of the reference answers are correct and belong to the requested category of the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

- 3) **Clarity of question** : whether the question is clear and concise. 

- 4) **Clarity of answers** : whether all the reference answers are clear and concise. 

- 5) **Relevance of question** : whether the question is within the scope of the specified lecture notes. 

- 6) **Relevance of answers** : whether all the answers are within the scope of the specified lecture notes. 

The human rater awarded a maximum of two points for each of the 6 criteria above, for a total of 12 points. Points were awarded depending on how well the question and its reference answers meet each criterion: 

- 1) **Not at all: 0 point** . For example, a question designated for the Create category, but asks student to recall a concept will be given 0 point for Validity. 

- 2) **Partially satisfactory: 1 point** . The question or answers might have some minor issues which require further modification before use. For example, some reference answers generated in our experiments, especially those under the Create category, provided additional details not covered in the lecture notes at all. 

- 3) **Entirely satisfactory: 2 points** . The question or answers are without any issues and can be used right away with no further modification. 

To mitigate the issue of not having a second rater, the following step-by-step evaluation process was followed to ensure the consistency of the ratings produced by the single human rater. 

- 1) The rater focuses on a single course topic at a time, such as software testing, to facilitate more accurate Bloom category assignment through comparison of questions within the same topic. 

- 2) The rater begins with questions in the simplest unrated Bloom category, Remember, which is one of the easiest cognitive levels to identify. The rater reads each question and evaluates its reference answers to assess validity, including correctness and appropriate Bloom category assignment. Points (0, 1, or 2) are then given accordingly. 

- 3) The rater then evaluates the clarity (clear, conciseness) of the question and answers. Points are given accordingly. 

- 4) The rater then refers to the relevant lecture notes to determine whether the question falls within the course scope and assigns points accordingly. 

- 5) After completing ratings for all questions within the same topic and Bloom category, the rater compares these questions and their ratings both against each other and against questions from the immediately preceding Bloom category to identify potential discrepancies. For example, an Apply question must assess students at a higher cognitive level than Understand by testing how they use information in new situations rather than just explaining concepts. The rater then adjusts the ratings if needed. 

- 6) The rater moves to the next Bloom category, e.g., Understand, in the same course topic and repeats steps 2-5.

sections.heading: _D. THREATS TO VALIDITY_
sections.text:
Like other empirical studies, the generalizability of our results is subject to a few threats as discussed below. 

First, this study employed a single human rater for the manual evaluation of generated questions. The rater is highly experienced in software engineering educational assessments. Such expertise, especially in highly specialized domains like software engineering education, can provide reliable evaluation of outputs generated by the agents in GenScore. However, we also recognized that including a second rater (who was not available to us during the time of the experiments) and reporting inter-rater metrics such as Krippendorff’s alpha might strengthen the reliability of this study. 

Second, outputs from LLMs could be changing from time to time due to their probabilistic nature. This would affect the quality of question generation, the rating of questions and the auto-scoring accuracy. We have mitigated this issue by generating and evaluating more than 300 new questions across 8 popular topics in software engineering and 6 different Bloom’s cognitive levels. We also used three different datasets with a total of more than 2800 answers to be auto-scored. At the same time, we recognize the importance of conducting the evaluation with more real-world datasets containing questions set at the higher cognitive levels of the Bloom categories, especially for the auto-scoring performance. Such datasets in software engineering courses are not available to us at the moment. 

Third, due to the budget and time constraints, we could not fully implement and evaluate the latest LLM models such as the reasoning models [38]. Newer and more expensive LLM models might improve the generation and auto-scoring performance compared to what have been reported in this 

work. As an extension of this work, we plan to run experiments with the latest LLM models such as OpenAI’s GPT-5 when the cost becomes more manageable and study if it improves the performance of rating agents when dealing with the higher cognitive levels of Bloom categories. In addition, we also plan to build rubric-based generators or discriminator enhancements designed specifically for higher Bloom levels such as _Evaluate_ and _Create_ , to improve our current rating agents. Such enhancements may produce better agreement between the human rater and the LLM-based agents. We note this area as an opportunity for possible improvement in our upcoming studies. 

Finally, we acknowledge that GenScore is primarily a proof of concept system. We plan to make it production-ready and evaluate it further in terms of system scalability and usability in real classroom deployments. In order not to cause possibly significant disruptions in student learning, such deployments will be complementary to existing classroom practices, i.e., students will have GenScore as an additional tool to practice new short answer questions in their own pace and get instant feedback. Based on the experimental results, we believe that it is necessary to include expert human oversight over practice questions generated by the system under the higher Bloom cognitive levels.

sections.heading: **VII. RELATED WORK**
sections.text:
Auto-generating assessments is an established research topic in technology-enabled education [39]. Existing work in this area have been focusing on various educational domains, such as reading comprehension question generation using natural language processing techniques [40], and more recently LLM based programming exercise generation [41], [42]. In [8], the authors applied LLMs and knowledge graphs to generate questions and answers for cybersecurity training. In [9], the authors performed automatic generation and evaluation of questions for content in Spanish. We have not come across works on auto-generating short-answer questions for software engineering courses. 

To the best of our knowledge, not much work has been done in generating short-answers questions that are aligned to the Bloom’s Taxonomy, which has been considered widely in educational assessment [43]. In [44], the authors investigated the problem of generating questions for the 6-level Boom’s Taxonomy based on the lecture material of an undergraduate software engineering course. The study evaluated 120 generated questions, but they were essay-type, not short-answer type of questions. In a more recent study [10], the authors used GPT-4 for Bloom-aligned multiple-choice, not shortanswer, question generation in a biology course. 

There have been recent research on the effectiveness of LLMs in generating assessment questions based on taxonomies such as Bloom’s. In [45], the authors conducted a human evaluation to assess the usefulness and quality of the questions generated by LLMs. The questions used in the evaluation were in the machine learning and biology domains, not software engineering. questions generated were of good quality. In GenScore, we implemented a multi-agent based approach to rate the generated questions and compared it to human-based rating. Our evaluation showed that it might be harder for LLMs to generate high quality questions at the higher cognitive levels such as _Evaluate_ or _Create_ in Bloom’s Taxonomy, especially in the more theory-oriented parts of software engineering courses. 

On the other hand, auto-scoring of short textual answers is a relatively more well-studied problem, especially with the recent development in LLMs [15]. Previous approaches made use of machine learning techniques [11], [12], [13], in which significant effort would be needed to manually engineer appropriate features for training the machine learning models. In [12], using the Mohler dataset [11] the authors considered different feature extraction techniques including text similarity, weights of terms, question demotion, etc., to develop regression models for auto-scoring short answers. In [13], various traditional machine learning models such as Random Forest and Support Vector Machines were trained on a subset of human-graded answers to classify the remaining answers. The results demonstrated significant reduction in manual workload in grading. Interestingly, in a recent work (2025), Boonsarngsuk et al. [46] found that simple reference answer sampling strategies such as K-means clustering and K-center outperformed existing similaritybased auto-scoring approaches. They achieved competitive performance compared to new LLM based approaches using OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini. Their datasets were collected from a Statistics and a Computer Architecture course at a university in Thailand. 

To reduce the manual feature engineering effort required in traditional machine learning, deep learning based methods for auto-scoring have become popular [32], [34], [36], [47]. Such models, e.g., text embedding, attention based neural networks, etc., have the ability to learn representative features directly from large datasets. In addition, manually crafted features could be incorporated in a complementary manner into deep learning models to enhance scoring accuracy [27]. We noted that deep learning based approaches require large, high quality datasets for proper model training and evaluation. 

With the recent rise of LLMs, naturally there have been more work on using them to perform auto-scoring of openended answers, for instance [14], [15], [16], [17]. Ta et al. [14] evaluated the performance of different OpenAI’s LLMs in scoring short-answer questions in software engineering courses, but did not consider an agent based approach nor the integration with question generation in a unified system to support learning. Other than that, not much work has been done for LLM-based auto-scoring of short answers in the context of computing education, especially in more theory-oriented software engineering courses. Research in auto-scoring of open-ended answers in computing education have been more involved with programming based questions [19], [48]. 

In other educational domains, Chang and Ginter [15] investigated the auto-scoring problem in Finnish based undergraduate courses using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The data was collected from different academic disciplines at the University of Turku. They found that GPT-4 (one-shot learning) provided the best performance. In [49], the authors implemented and evaluated few-shot pre-trained language models for the automatic essay scoring task. We noted that grading essays is quite different from short-answer scoring, as the former requires the evaluation of different criteria such as text coherence and organization, logical arguments, etc. The authors of [50] evaluated GPT-4 for short answer grading using the SciEntsBank and Beetle datasets. They found that for these datasets, GPT-4’s performance is comparable to manually crafted machine learning models. ChatGPT was used in [51] to correct open-ended answers in technical training of professional software developers. We noted that existing approaches did not attempt to investigate the auto-scoring performance with respect to various cognitive levels in the Bloom’s Taxonomy. 

**Summary** : Our approach presents several main novelties over existing LLM-based educational tools. First, GenScore integrates question generation and auto-scoring in a unified system for software engineering education, whereas existing work treats these as separate problems. Second, we target short-answer questions aligned to Bloom’s Taxonomy for theory-oriented software engineering courses. Prior work has focused on other assessment formats (essays, multiple-choice, programming exercises) or other educational domains. Third, we evaluate both question generation quality and scoring performance across Bloom’s cognitive levels. Our experiments revealed that LLMs struggle more with creating questions for higher-order thinking skills such as Evaluate and Create in software engineering contexts. This taxonomy-based performance analysis for both generation and scoring has not been explored in prior research in automated assessments.

sections.heading: **VIII. CONCLUSION**
sections.text:
In this work, we developed a practical, automated short answer question generation and answer scoring system, named GenScore, which can be used by both instructors and students in the context of software engineering courses. GenScore involves the use of LLM agents which can perform complex tasks based on customized prompts and relevant tool usage, e.g., to extract context from suitable lecture notes for enhancing generation and scoring performance. In this way, GenScore can be used for question generation and scoring for a wide variety of courses if the relevant course materials are provided, not just for software engineering courses. 

We conducted extensive experiments to investigate the auto-generation and auto-scoring capabilities of GenScore. We used a large number of course topics and questions/answers from various datasets including publicly available and our own datasets. The results demonstrated

GenScore can easily incorporate new AI techniques and models, which are being introduced on a weekly basis these days, to further reduce workload for instructors in tedious question creation and grading tasks.
